The foundations chapter derived [Bayes' rule](../foundations/bayes-rule.qmd), and the frequentist sequence distinguished a [likelihood from a probability distribution over observations](maximum-likelihood.qmd). We now combine the two to construct a posterior distribution from an observed linguistic resource.

## An exchangeable Bernoulli superpopulation model

We use the Turkish table from the [UniMorph release pinned at commit `6c179ac`](https://github.com/unimorph/tur/tree/6c179ace7d2f3d7f3484020e5304c1544d07bb6b). Pimentel et al. ([2021](https://aclanthology.org/2021.sigmorphon-1.25/)) describe its use in a morphological-reinflection task, and Batsuren et al. ([2022](https://aclanthology.org/2022.lrec-1.89/)) describe UniMorph as a type-level resource of lemma--form--feature triples. The data are CC BY-SA 3.0.

The course table retains 588 distinct verb lexemes with one form in the feature cell `V;IND;PST;3;SG;POS;DECL`. A row is a lexeme--paradigm cell, not a usage token. The binary variable $Z_i$ marks whether the course-derived two-character ending begins with *t*. This ending is an orthographic measurement, not a UniMorph morpheme boundary.

```{r}
#| label: load-unimorph-posterior
library(ggplot2)

population <- read.csv(
  "data/unimorph-turkish/verb-past-population.csv",
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)
sample_120 <- read.csv(
  "data/unimorph-turkish/verb-past-sample-120.csv",
  stringsAsFactors = FALSE
)

N <- nrow(population)
K <- sum(population$t_initial)
n <- nrow(sample_120)
k <- sum(sample_120$t_initial)
resource_share <- K / N

stopifnot(
  N == 588L, K == 200L, n == 120L, k == 42L,
  !anyDuplicated(population$lemma),
  all(sample_120$lemma %in% population$lemma)
)

data.frame(N, K, n, k, resource_share, sample_share = k / n)
```

The value $K/N=$ `r sprintf("%.6f", resource_share)` is known because the complete pinned resource is available. There is no posterior uncertainty about that finite-population proportion.

To introduce Bayesian updating, we posit an exchangeable superpopulation from which lexeme cells are independently drawn,

$$
Z_i\mid\Theta=\theta
\overset{\mathrm{iid}}{\sim}
\operatorname{Bernoulli}(\theta),
\qquad
\Theta\sim\operatorname{Beta}(1,1).
$$

This exchangeable Bernoulli superpopulation model is counterfactual, not a description of the actual sampling design. The committed 120-row sample was drawn without replacement from the known 588-row resource, so independent Bernoulli sampling does not describe that procedure.

## Updating a continuous parameter

Bayes' rule for a continuous parameter is

$$
f_{\Theta\mid\mathbf Z}(\theta\mid\mathbf z)
=
\frac{
p_{\mathbf Z\mid\Theta}(\mathbf z\mid\theta)f_\Theta(\theta)
}{
p_{\mathbf Z}(\mathbf z)
}.
$$

The denominator

$$
p_{\mathbf Z}(\mathbf z)
=
\int_0^1
p_{\mathbf Z\mid\Theta}(\mathbf z\mid\theta)
f_\Theta(\theta)\,\mathrm d\theta
$$

normalizes the numerator. For $k$ focal cells among $n$ exchangeable Bernoulli observations, the likelihood kernel is

$$
p_{\mathbf Z\mid\Theta}(\mathbf z\mid\theta)
\propto
\theta^k(1-\theta)^{n-k}.
$$

Multiplying by the $\operatorname{Beta}(1,1)$ prior gives

$$
f_{\Theta\mid\mathbf Z}(\theta\mid\mathbf z)
\propto
\theta^{1+k-1}(1-\theta)^{1+n-k-1},
$$

so the exchangeable Bernoulli superpopulation model posterior is

$$
\Theta\mid\mathbf z
\sim
\operatorname{Beta}(1+k,1+n-k).
$$

```{r}
#| label: compute-unimorph-posterior
prior_alpha <- 1
prior_beta <- 1
posterior_alpha <- prior_alpha + k
posterior_beta <- prior_beta + n - k

theta_grid <- seq(0, 1, length.out = 1001L)
posterior_density <- data.frame(
  theta = theta_grid,
  prior = dbeta(theta_grid, prior_alpha, prior_beta),
  posterior = dbeta(theta_grid, posterior_alpha, posterior_beta)
)

stopifnot(posterior_alpha == 43L, posterior_beta == 79L)
data.frame(posterior_alpha, posterior_beta)
```

The 42 observed *t*-initial cells and 78 other cells update the prior to a beta distribution with shape parameters `r posterior_alpha` and `r posterior_beta`.

```{r}
#| label: plot-unimorph-posterior
#| fig-cap: "Prior and exchangeable Bernoulli superpopulation model posterior densities. The vertical line is the known proportion in the pinned resource, not an uncertain parameter estimate."
posterior_long <- rbind(
  data.frame(theta = theta_grid, density = posterior_density$prior,
             distribution = "prior"),
  data.frame(theta = theta_grid, density = posterior_density$posterior,
             distribution = "posterior")
)

ggplot(posterior_long, aes(theta, density, linetype = distribution)) +
  geom_line(color = "#8B1A1A", linewidth = 0.85) +
  geom_vline(xintercept = resource_share, color = "grey35", linewidth = 0.6) +
  labs(x = "Modeled share of lexeme cells with a t-initial ending",
       y = "Density", linetype = NULL) +
  theme_classic(base_size = 12) +
  theme(legend.position = "top")
```

For a continuous parameter, the density at one point is not a point probability. Posterior probabilities are integrals over intervals:

$$
\mathbb{P}(a<\Theta<b\mid\mathbf z)
=
\int_a^b
f_{\Theta\mid\mathbf Z}(\theta\mid\mathbf z)\,\mathrm d\theta.
$$

The shorter statement $f(\theta\mid\mathbf z)\propto p(\mathbf z\mid\theta)f(\theta)$ identifies posterior shape, but a normalized density is required before we assign such probabilities.

## What the posterior does not say

The likelihood evaluates the fixed sample as a function of $\theta$; the posterior distributes model-based uncertainty over $\theta$ after conditioning on that sample. Neither quantity changes the known resource proportion. UniMorph supplies types, not token frequencies, so this posterior does not estimate the frequency of *t*-initial past endings in Turkish use.

## Check your understanding

1. Which quantity is fixed when the likelihood is evaluated?
2. Why is $200/588$ not uncertain in this analysis?
3. Which assumption makes the exchangeable Bernoulli superpopulation model a counterfactual superpopulation model rather than a description of the committed sample?
4. Why is a posterior density at one value not a point probability?

<details class="understanding-answers">
<summary>Answers</summary>

1. The observed sample $\mathbf z$, including $n=120$ and $k=42$, is fixed while the likelihood varies over $\theta$. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
2. The complete pinned resource is observed, so its 200 focal rows and 588 total rows are fixed counts rather than uncertain parameters. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
3. The exchangeable Bernoulli superpopulation model assumes independent, exchangeable Bernoulli draws from a superpopulation, while the committed sample was drawn without replacement from the known finite resource. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->
4. For a continuous parameter, probability is an integral over an interval; a density value at one point is not probability mass at that point. <!-- dqr-allow: empirical-answer -->

</details>

The [posterior-summaries page](posterior-summaries.qmd) extracts several distinct claims from this posterior.
